det_01.label: TidyTuesday 2020-01-07: an emergency dataset release
det_01.content: This dataset was released as part of TidyTuesday on 7 January 2020, in the middle of an active disaster. The official readme explicitly tells users to be cautious when plotting: the NSW Rural Fire Service major-incidents JSON was downloaded on 2020-01-06, and a NASA MODIS active-fire snapshot covers the seven days leading up to release. It was assembled less to drive a polished analysis than to let the data community see what was happening in real time. Unlike most TidyTuesday weeks that ship a single tidy CSV, this one bundles three very different sources: NASA satellite hotspots, NSW RFS incident polygons, and decades of Bureau of Meteorology weather records, with the South-East as the area most affected.

det_02.label: Black Summer: the season behind the data
det_02.content: The 2019-20 Australian bushfire season — known as the Black Summer — burned roughly 24 million hectares of land, an area larger than the United Kingdom. Thirty-three people died directly in the fires; an additional ~417 deaths were attributed to bushfire smoke. Around 3,094 homes were destroyed. The wildlife toll, the most cited number from this event, is approximately 3 billion native vertebrates killed or displaced (mostly reptiles), with up to 60,000 koalas affected and an estimated 40,000 koalas perishing on Kangaroo Island alone. The fire pixels in the MODIS file are this season — sampled in its first week.

det_03.label: 2019: hottest and driest year on record
det_03.content: 2019 was simultaneously Australia's hottest and driest year on record — the first time since overlapping records began that both extremes occurred in the same calendar year. Annual mean temperature was 1.52 °C above the 1961-1990 average, the previous record (1.33 °C, 2013) shattered. Maximum temperatures ran +2.09 °C above the long-term average — the first time the country crossed a +2 °C anomaly. Area-averaged rainfall was just 277.6 mm against a long-term average of 465.2 mm. For the first time, every single month of the year was below the national rainfall average. This is the climatological pre-condition the fire data sits on top of.

det_04.label: MODIS FIRMS: how to read fire pixels honestly
det_04.content: The fire data is from NASA's FIRMS / MODIS Collection 6 active-fire product. A row is not a fire — it is a 1 km satellite pixel that was thermally anomalous when MODIS passed overhead. NASA explicitly warns that FIRMS active fires should not be used to estimate burned area, because of nontrivial spatial and temporal sampling. MODIS detects roughly a quarter of fires recorded by ground agencies in the contiguous US; small under-canopy fires often go undetected because the canopy hides the heat signature. Because the MODIS bands do not perfectly distinguish heat sources, occasional pixels are gas flares, volcanic vents, or hot industrial roofs, not vegetation fire. Confidence is graded low / nominal / high, day or night. Daytime detections also pick up reflective surfaces, so the readme suggests night data for highest accuracy. Every chart we draw must respect this: we are mapping satellite detections, not ground truth.

det_05.label: Sydney's smoke crisis: PM2.5 at 11x hazardous
det_05.content: On 10 December 2019, Sydney's air-quality index hit roughly 11 times the threshold considered hazardous, with PM2.5 around 400 µg/m³ — almost 40 times the WHO guideline. The same day, NSW emergency departments saw 234 asthma and breathing-problem presentations against an average of 130. Subsequent peer-reviewed work estimated each 0–10 µg/m³ rise in bushfire-derived PM2.5 raised three-day all-cause mortality risk by ~3.2 %, concentrated in people aged 65 and over. The Black Summer's invisible casualty count — about 417 smoke-attributed deaths — comes from this kind of exposure-response statistic, not from the fire-line itself.

det_06.label: Climate attribution: a 30%+ rise in fire weather risk
det_06.content: The World Weather Attribution rapid-attribution study found that anthropogenic climate change has raised the Fire Weather Index in the affected region by at least 30 %, driven mostly by extreme heat. Heat extremes of the 2019-20 magnitude have become at least twice as likely under long-term warming. The drought that primed the fuel had a more complex story — a coincidence of two consecutive positive Indian Ocean Dipole events with a Central Pacific El Niño, which climate change is making more frequent. The conclusion: the fire weather of Black Summer is not a one-off; it is what an early-21st-century Australian summer can now look like.

det_07.label: Six cities, one continent: the BoM weather panel
det_07.content: The Bureau of Meteorology data in this dataset is not a national average — it is six (sometimes seven) hand-picked stations near the largest cities: Perth (Subiaco WWTP, 009151), Adelaide (North Adelaide, 023011), Brisbane (Greenslopes Hospital, 040383, plus Brisbane city 040913), Sydney (Observatory Hill, 066062), Canberra (Airport, 070351) and Melbourne (Botanical Gardens, 086232). Observatory Hill, in particular, has rainfall back to 1858 and temperature back to 1859 — among the longest continuous urban records in the Southern Hemisphere. Most of the climate signal in this analysis is therefore the South-East corner of Australia, exactly the region the readme flags as 'most affected'.

det_08.label: NSW Rural Fire Service: the ground-truth complement
det_08.content: The majorIncidents-2020-01-06.json file is from the NSW Rural Fire Service public feed — it is the agency's own list of active incidents the moment the dataset was published. Unlike satellite hotspots, an RFS record corresponds to a real reported incident with a status (Out of Control / Being Controlled / Under Control), an alert level, a location, and often a description. Pairing this with MODIS lets a story confirm: when satellites saw a hotspot in the South East coast, RFS was almost certainly running an active incident on the ground. The RFS feed is the link between abstract pixels and the people and equipment fighting them.

det_09.label: Hectares vs satellite pixels: the scale gap
det_09.content: The two fire products in this dataset measure different things. The seven-day MODIS file is a snapshot — bright pixels in a one-week window. The full Black Summer burned-area total of ~24 million hectares is a season-long ground accounting from agencies. A 1 km MODIS pixel covers ~100 hectares; if we naively multiplied the ~34,000 detection rows by 100 ha we would massively overcount, because the same fire is re-detected on every overpass and many pixels overlap. The benchmark to use is the official seasonal total, not the satellite count. The dataset is a slice of an event whose full scale is documented elsewhere.
